\begin{abstract}
Coding agents delegate work to \emph{subagents}: named helpers defined in version-controlled Markdown
files that also list the tools each may use. We study \nSpecsEng{} such specifications in \nReposEng{} engineered
GitHub repositories. We execute the coding tool to obtain its effective grants. In the average repository, \RQthreeIncoherentEng{} of explicit grants that omit every
file-writing tool keep an unscoped shell (\nDomSpecs{} specifications in \nDomRepos{} repositories). Wherever shell
commands run without per-command approval and without a sandbox, such grants withhold permission but not authority.
Specifications that a model annotated as meant to inspect hold file-writing tools \RQtwoRoleGapWrite{} less often
than those meant to change code, but only \RQtwoRoleGapAuthority{} less often once the shell is counted, and the text
of most write-withholding grants that keep a shell asks it at most to read or verify. An experiment of
\nExpRuns{} delegations across three models, with shell commands approved automatically,
checks the mechanism: with the most common inspection grant and no prompt restriction, requested file changes
succeeded in \ExpCtwoRate{} of runs. A prompt restriction held for Sonnet and Opus but not reliably for Haiku, and
Haiku without a shell sometimes reported changes it had not made. In \nOverRuns{} report-only delegations on one small
fixture, no agent changed a file, and a command pattern such as \code{Bash(git log:*)} in a
subagent's tool list did not stop it from writing files. The runtime also drops unresolved tool names silently. We release the corpus, oracles and a linter.
\keywords{agentic software engineering \and AI teammates \and mining software repositories \and
configuration defects \and delegation \and least privilege \and capability security}
\end{abstract}

\paragraph{Data availability}
The corpus (\nSpecsAll{} specifications with their raw frontmatter, the per-repository configuration
inventories, repository metadata, the oracle transcripts and the annotation batches), the tool
vocabulary established across \nReleasesHistory{} releases, the experiments' run records, and the
complete analysis output are archived at Zenodo \authornote{DOI to be minted before submission} and
maintained at \url{\repourl}. Every file was fetched by its git blob identifier and verified by hash,
so the release is the snapshot rather than a later state.

\paragraph{Code availability}
The collection and reconstruction scripts, the executable oracles, the annotation tooling and
codebooks, the analysis, the figure scripts and the linter are released in the same archive and at
\url{\repourl}. Code is licensed under the MIT licence and the corpus under CC~BY~4.0.

\paragraph{Acknowledgements and use of generative AI}
Claude Code, with Claude Opus models, was used to write and run the collection, oracle and analysis code, to check
citations and claims against their sources, and to draft and revise the manuscript text. The authors reviewed the
code, the analysis and the text, and take full responsibility for the content of the article. Language models are
also part of the study design, as annotators (\S\ref{sec:annotation}) and as experimental subjects
(\S\ref{sec:experiment}); the model versions, codebooks, prompts and labels are reported there and released.
